📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've stated it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

According to recent reports, the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

Industry observers note that we'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a significant, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Industry observers note that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

Industry observers note that with that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

Industry observers note that while we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I noted, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

It has been revealed that I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of crucial ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

According to recent reports, pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

Recent findings suggest that for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

It has been revealed that after a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

In a recent development, all of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a fresh player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

Sources indicate that indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Recent findings suggest that over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot newly introduced thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In a recent development, in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

In a recent development, early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

Industry observers note that when it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint problem in bright ambient light.

Industry observers note that if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

It has been revealed that not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the latest RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

Sources indicate that the long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the newly introduced 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of concerns like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

In a recent development, really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, presently, be entirely sure about that.

In a recent development, second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

While you wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, you owe it to yourself to play Tainted Grail

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Dungeon Master, PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Dungeon Master, PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.

Recent findings suggest that I will probably be in the ground when Bethesda finally releases The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel—which is kind of liberating. I have hype immunity. But what's even more liberating is the fact that there's already an RPG that does everything I want from an Elder Scrolls game—2025's Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avelon.

Tainted Grail is unabashedly created in the mould of The Elder Scrolls, in that it is a primarily first-person fantasy RPG where flexibility is its superpower. You chart your own course and effectively construct your class, enhancing skills by using them as much as possible. But it is not merely the Elder Scrolls we have at home—it captures the very best that this kind of RPG can offer, and in some ways manages to outdo Bethesda.

Industry observers note that this is apparent right from the get-go. In classic Elder Scrolls form, Tainted Grail begins with you banged up in a facility that incarcerates and studies unfortunates afflicted with a magical plague, of which you are one. Follow the critical path and you will meet a new friend, get in some tough fights and then escape.

By the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.

But this island asylum is substantial. Really big. It's full of locked doors, hidden rooms, large spaces ripe for some big brawls, a subterranean area waiting to be delved into, oodles of lore—there are hours of rooting around to be done. So I ignored the critical path, had a big old wander, and by the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.

While Tainted Grail is full of bespoke quests sending you off into the open world on countless adventures, these are really just designed to get you out the door so you can stumble upon something cool—a latest enemy that will utterly destroy you, a powerful weapon hidden in a crypt, an eccentric immortal being who wants to make a deal. The vibe is very TTRPG, which isn't surprising, given that it's based on one.

According to recent reports, and these adventures are actually dangerous. Deadly, even. The villains of Tainted Grail hit hard, and early on you will feel horrifyingly vulnerable. Basic bandits and skeletons can easily spell your doom. And if you stay out at night, you're screwed. Avelon is a miserable, cruel place, cursed and plagued, and you will struggle.

Industry observers note that developer Questline didn't simply up the lethality and call it a day, though. Tainted Grail, unlike The Elder Scrolls, actually has a quality combat system that falls firmly into the skill-based category. It's no Dark Souls, but it's more Dark Souls than Skyrim. So that increased level of challenge feels earned because of the tools you have available to you, and the range of combat styles you can develop.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Recent findings suggest that with all the options you have at your disposal—which has been further enhanced by DLC additions, letting you, for example, go through this Arthurian fantasy RPG as a kung-fu master—it can be hard to commit to a build. I've been spellblading it up, with my alchemical skills helping to shore up my weaknesses, but every time I encounter a newly introduced piece of gear I wonder what else I could create. But you do need to commit eventually. This isn't a game for a jack of all trades.

Industry observers note that while Bethesda is more deft at crafting believable, reactive lands, Tainted Grail's world design also deserves its flowers. It's a smaller space, divided into three main areas, and while you can absolutely muck around for hundreds of hours, you can experience most of what it has to offer in 50. But what you'll experience in those 50 hours is so much more meticulously designed, with Questline getting so much out of each location.

It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions.

It's a looker, too. What it lacks in fidelity it more than makes up for in the art design department, and it's another place where Dark Souls rears its gorgeously hideous head. Tainted Grail finds beauty in the grim misery of its fantastical post-apocalyptic realm. It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions—the arboreal and the horrific, the grounded and alien. Avelon is delightfully strange, and that makes exploration all the more thrilling.

In a recent development, as games grow ever larger and more bloated, my appreciation for richer, better-scoped worlds like Avalon only grows. And this does not indicate a dearth of ambition on Questline's part. Tainted Grail is a complex, elaborate game that will happily devour your days and keep showing you upcoming things.

Industry observers note that clearly people want this—Tainted Grail has done very well for itself, garnering more than 20,000 user reviews on Steam, where its rating sits at Very Positive. It's a reassuring reminder that you do not need a gargantuan studio and big publisher money to make a quality RPG in the Elder Scrolls style.

Sources indicate that we don't know how many people are working on Sentinel right now, but we can expect the number to be large. Skyrim had around 100 people working on it, and with Starfield that jumped to more than 400. Tainted Grail was made by 50 people. That's quite the achievement.

It has been revealed that so if you're craving a side-quest-heavy sandbox RPG with plenty of sword fights and spellflinging, Tainted Grail should absolutely be your next port of call. And the good news is that there's a demo. No excuses. Go play it.
